sentences.text: The jaws of this creature were straight and pointed, resembling those found in Quetzalcoatlus and Zhejiangopterus.
Bony bumps on the jaw hint at unique functions, perhaps for showing off, holding soft tissue, or crushing hard shells.
Fossils were found at Aferdou N'Chaft, near the village of Begaa, during excavations in the Kem Kem Beds that took place in April and from November to December 2008.
Wellnhofer and Buffetaut originally described two jaw fragments in 1999 without assigning them a formal name.
The name Alanqa derives from the Arabic term al-'anqā', which refers to a mythical bird comparable to the Persian Simurgh.
Comparisons with related species suggest that individuals known from jaw specimens likely possessed wingspans of about 4 meters.
A vertebra possibly belonging to the same species indicates an individual with a wingspan of about 6 meters.
This animal was likely prey for large predators including Spinosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, Sauroniops, Aegisuchus, and possibly an unidentified madtsoiid snake.
Alanqa was initially placed in the Azhdarchidae family due to jaw similarities with Quetzalcoatlus and Zhejiangopterus.
A 2022 study recovered Alanqa as a basal azhdarchoid related to Keresdrakon, forming the new clade Alanqidae.
Alanqa lived about 95 million years ago during the Cenomanian stage in what is now southeastern Morocco.
It inhabited a freshwater delta system between 100.5 and 93.9 million years ago during the late Cenomanian.
A 2018 analysis suggested Alanqa was a thalassodromid, but this classification is not well-supported.
